claim: In the adult small intestine, cells from a common progenitor intermix with other lineages.
source: In the adult small intestine, cells from a common progenitor intermix with other lineages, whereas cell progeny in many other epithelia form contiguous patches.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known characteristic of the adult small intestine.

claim: Cell progeny in many epithelia form contiguous patches.
source: In the adult small intestine, cells from a common progenitor intermix with other lineages, whereas cell progeny in many other epithelia form contiguous patches.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known characteristic of many epithelia.

claim: Lineages intersperse during cytokinesis in intestinal organoids.
source: Using light sheet and confocal imaging of intestinal organoids, we show that lineages intersperse during cytokinesis, when elongated interphase cells insert between apically displaced daughters.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' light sheet and confocal imaging experiments.

claim: Elongated interphase cells insert between apically displaced daughters during cytokinesis.
source: Using light sheet and confocal imaging of intestinal organoids, we show that lineages intersperse during cytokinesis, when elongated interphase cells insert between apically displaced daughters.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments describing the mechanism of interspersion.

claim: Reducing the cellular aspect ratio disrupts interspersion, producing contiguous patches.
source: Reducing the cellular aspect ratio to minimize the height difference between interphase and mitotic cells disrupts interspersion, producing contiguous patches.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments manipulating cellular aspect ratio.

claim: Cellular aspect ratio is a key parameter for division-coupled interspersion in the early mouse embryo.
source: Cellular aspect ratio is similarly a key parameter for division-coupled interspersion in the early mouse embryo, suggesting that this physical mechanism for patterning progeny may pertain to many mammalian epithelia.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments in early mouse embryos.

claim: The physical mechanism for patterning progeny may pertain to many mammalian epithelia.
source: Cellular aspect ratio is similarly a key parameter for division-coupled interspersion in the early mouse embryo, suggesting that this physical mechanism for patterning progeny may pertain to many mammalian epithelia.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the authors' findings in intestinal organoids and early mouse embryos.

claim: The process of cytokinesis in elongated mammalian epithelia allows lineages to intermix.
source: Our results reveal that the process of cytokinesis in elongated mammalian epithelia allows lineages to intermix and that cellular aspect ratio is a critical modulator of the progeny pattern.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the authors' experiments.

claim: Cellular aspect ratio is a critical modulator of the progeny pattern.
source: Our results reveal that the process of cytokinesis in elongated mammalian epithelia allows lineages to intermix and that cellular aspect ratio is a critical modulator of the progeny pattern.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the authors' experiments.

claim: The adult mammalian small intestine contains many cell types and maintains a high degree of spatial organization during rapid turnover.
source: The adult mammalian small intestine is a prime example of an epithelium that contains many cell types and maintains a high degree of spatial organization during rapid turnover (Barker, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Barker, 2014.

claim: Divisions of stem cells in the crypts of Lieberkühn replenish the stem cell pool and generate absorptive and secretory progenitor cells.
source: In the small intestine, divisions of stem cells in the crypts of Lieberkühn replenish the stem cell pool and generate absorptive and secretory progenitor cells in the crypt, which in turn produce differentiated cells that carry out the absorptive and protective functions of the gut (Gracz and Magness, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gracz and Magness, 2014.

claim: Absorptive and secretory progenitor cells produce differentiated cells that carry out the absorptive and protective functions of the gut.
source: In the small intestine, divisions of stem cells in the crypts of Lieberkühn replenish the stem cell pool and generate absorptive and secretory progenitor cells in the crypt, which in turn produce differentiated cells that carry out the absorptive and protective functions of the gut (Gracz and Magness, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gracz and Magness, 2014.

claim: Cells derived from a given progenitor intersperse with other cells throughout the intestinal epithelium.
source: Throughout the epithelium, cells derived from a given progenitor intersperse with other cells (Carroll et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carroll et al., 2017.

claim: Lineage tracing in fixed tissues has established that cells derived from secretory progenitors intermix with cells derived from absorptive progenitors along the crypt and villus length.
source: In particular, lineage tracing in fixed tissues has established that cells derived from secretory progenitors intermix with cells derived from absorptive progenitors along the crypt and villus length (Yang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2001.

claim: At the crypt base, stem cells are interspersed with Paneth cells.
source: At the crypt base, stem cells are interspersed with Paneth cells (Farin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Farin et al., 2016.

claim: Interspersion of cell lineages plays important roles in determining local signaling environments required for intestinal homeostasis.
source: Interspersion of cell lineages plays important roles in determining local signaling environments required for intestinal homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Intestinal stem cells receive signals critical to their identity from neighboring Paneth cells.
source: For example, intestinal stem cells receive signals critical to their identity from neighboring Paneth cells (Sato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sato et al., 2011.

claim: Direct contact between stem and Paneth cells supports stem cell maintenance.
source: Indeed, direct contact between stem and Paneth cells supports stem cell maintenance (Farin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Farin et al., 2016.

claim: The molecular mechanisms that underlie the intermixing of lineages are poorly understood.
source: However, the molecular mechanisms that underlie the intermixing of lineages are poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Rearrangements of the actin cytoskeleton displace mitotic cells along the apical-basal axis.
source: We find that rearrangements of the actin cytoskeleton displace mitotic cells along the apical-basal axis, such that cell division occurs at the apical surface.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments.

claim: Cell division occurs at the apical surface in intestinal organoids.
source: We find that rearrangements of the actin cytoskeleton displace mitotic cells along the apical-basal axis, such that cell division occurs at the apical surface.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments.

claim: Interspersion arises when elongated interphase neighboring cells wedge between apically dividing daughters during cytokinesis.
source: Interspersion arises when elongated interphase neighboring cells wedge between apically dividing daughters during cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments describing the mechanism of interspersion.

claim: The propensity to intersperse during division requires an elongated shape of cells in the epithelium.
source: We find that the propensity to intersperse during division requires an elongated shape of cells in the epithelium; reducing the cellular aspect ratio (height: width) in organoids disrupts interspersion, resulting in outgrowth of lineage patches.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments manipulating cellular aspect ratio.

claim: The physical parameters of the tissue are a critical determinant of interspersion during division.
source: Consistent with our data indicating that the physical parameters of the tissue are a critical determinant of interspersion during division, we demonstrate that the elongated epiblast/primitive ectoderm of post-implantation (E7.5) mouse embryos, but not the short visceral endoderm, also undergoes division-coupled cell interspersion.
evidence: This is inferred from the authors' data showing that elongated cells intersperse while short cells do not.

claim: The elongated epiblast/primitive ectoderm of post-implantation (E7.5) mouse embryos undergoes division-coupled cell interspersion.
source: Consistent with our data indicating that the physical parameters of the tissue are a critical determinant of interspersion during division, we demonstrate that the elongated epiblast/primitive ectoderm of post-implantation (E7.5) mouse embryos, but not the short visceral endoderm, also undergoes division-coupled cell interspersion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments in early mouse embryos.

claim: The short visceral endoderm of post-implantation (E7.5) mouse embryos does not undergo division-coupled cell interspersion.
source: Consistent with our data indicating that the physical parameters of the tissue are a critical determinant of interspersion during division, we demonstrate that the elongated epiblast/primitive ectoderm of post-implantation (E7.5) mouse embryos, but not the short visceral endoderm, also undergoes division-coupled cell interspersion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments in early mouse embryos.

claim: Tissues of distinct developmental context from the adult small intestine exhibit similar mechanisms for patterning cellular progeny according to cellular dimensions.
source: Thus, tissues of distinct developmental context from the adult small intestine exhibit similar mechanisms for patterning cellular progeny according to cellular dimensions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' experiments in intestinal organoids and early mouse embryos.

claim: Cell shape differences between interphase and mitotic cells in elongated mammalian epithelia can allow a neighboring cell to insert between nascent daughter cells during cytokinesis.
source: Together, our data indicate that cell shape differences between interphase and mitotic cells in elongated mammalian epithelia can allow a neighboring cell to insert between nascent daughter cells during cytokinesis and drive interspersion of cellular progeny.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the authors' experiments.

claim: Cell shape differences between interphase and mitotic cells drive interspersion of cellular progeny.
source: Together, our data indicate that cell shape differences between interphase and mitotic cells in elongated mammalian epithelia can allow a neighboring cell to insert between nascent daughter cells during cytokinesis and drive interspersion of cellular progeny.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the authors' experiments.

claim: Daughter cells separated from one another in approximately half of divisions in Atoh1-expressing secretory cells.
source: Strikingly, we observed that daughter cells separated from one another in approximately half of divisions (31/50 divisions, Figure 1A and Video 1; also see [Carroll et al., 2017]).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Atoh1-expressing secretory daughters along the crypt length separated from one another, mixing with unlabeled cells.
source: We observed that Atoh1-expressing secretory daughters along the crypt length separated from one another, mixing with unlabeled cells (Figure 1A and Video 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: 3D SPIM data confirmed that cells were fully separated on their basal surface.
source: 3D SPIM data confirmed that cells were fully separated on their basal surface, although they maintained a minimal contact on the apical surface, creating a V-shaped geometry (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Figure 1—video 1, 9/16 daughter pairs).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' 3D SPIM imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, and Figure 1—video 1.

claim: Separated daughter cells maintained a minimal contact on the apical surface, creating a V-shaped geometry.
source: 3D SPIM data confirmed that cells were fully separated on their basal surface, although they maintained a minimal contact on the apical surface, creating a V-shaped geometry (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Figure 1—video 1, 9/16 daughter pairs).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' 3D SPIM imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, and Figure 1—video 1.

claim: When daughters did not separate during the division, these daughters either became separated at later time points by division of a neighboring cell, or remained as neighbors for the duration of imaging.
source: When daughters did not separate during the division (Figure 1D, top panels, 7/16 daughter pairs), these daughters either became separated at later time points by division of a neighboring cell (Figure 1D, bottom panels and Figure 1—video 2), or remained as neighbors for the duration of imaging.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1D and Figure 1—video 2.

claim: Separation of nascent daughter cells during cell division makes substantial contributions to the relative positioning of cell types within the intestinal epithelium.
source: These data indicate that separation of nascent daughter cells during cell division makes substantial contributions to the relative positioning of cell types within the intestinal epithelium.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' imaging experiments.

claim: Mixing occurred as cells underwent cytokinesis on the apical surface of the epithelium, during which neighboring cells intruded within the ingressing cytokinetic furrow.
source: We observed that mixing occurred as cells underwent cytokinesis on the apical surface of the epithelium, during which neighboring cells intruded within the ingressing cytokinetic furrow (Figure 1B, Video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1B and Video 2.

claim: Mitotic cells displaced to the apical surface of the epithelium.
source: First, mitotic cells displaced to the apical surface of the epithelium, and the dramatic reduction in their basal footprint caused neighboring cells to reposition and occupy the position above (basal to) the mitotic cell (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The dramatic reduction in the basal footprint of mitotic cells caused neighboring cells to reposition and occupy the position above (basal to) the mitotic cell.
source: First, mitotic cells displaced to the apical surface of the epithelium, and the dramatic reduction in their basal footprint caused neighboring cells to reposition and occupy the position above (basal to) the mitotic cell (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells progressed through a polarized (non-concentric) cytokinesis.
source: Cells progressed through a polarized (non-concentric) cytokinesis (Figure 2A, Video 2, Figure 2—videos 1, 2 and 3) (also see [Fleming et al., 2007]), in which the cleavage furrow initiated from the basal surface and then progressed to the apical surface.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 2A, Video 2, and Figure 2—videos 1, 2 and 3, and supported by a citation to Fleming et al., 2007.

claim: The cleavage furrow initiated from the basal surface and then progressed to the apical surface.
source: Cells progressed through a polarized (non-concentric) cytokinesis (Figure 2A, Video 2, Figure 2—videos 1, 2 and 3) (also see [Fleming et al., 2007]), in which the cleavage furrow initiated from the basal surface and then progressed to the apical surface.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 2A, Video 2, and Figure 2—videos 1, 2 and 3, and supported by a citation to Fleming et al., 2007.

claim: As cytokinesis continued, a minimal daughter-daughter contact remained on the apical surface.
source: As cytokinesis continued, a minimal daughter-daughter contact remained on the apical surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The minimal vertex contact between daughters is consistent with other reports of daughter cell geometry during vertebrate cytokinesis.
source: We note that this minimal vertex contact is consistent with other reports of daughter cell geometry during vertebrate cytokinesis (Higashi et al., 2016), but contrasts with the long daughter-daughter interface generated during cytokinesis in Drosophila epithelia (Gibson et al., 2006; Herszterg et al., 2013; Pinheiro et al., 2017), as we will return to in the Discussion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Higashi et al., 2016, Gibson et al., 2006, Herszterg et al., 2013, and Pinheiro et al., 2017.

claim: The minimal vertex contact between daughters contrasts with the long daughter-daughter interface generated during cytokinesis in Drosophila epithelia.
source: We note that this minimal vertex contact is consistent with other reports of daughter cell geometry during vertebrate cytokinesis (Higashi et al., 2016), but contrasts with the long daughter-daughter interface generated during cytokinesis in Drosophila epithelia (Gibson et al., 2006; Herszterg et al., 2013; Pinheiro et al., 2017), as we will return to in the Discussion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gibson et al., 2006, Herszterg et al., 2013, and Pinheiro et al., 2017.

claim: The minimal contact between daughters generated by cytokinesis allowed a neighboring interphase cell to wedge between the daughters.
source: The minimal contact between daughters generated by cytokinesis allowed a neighboring interphase cell to wedge between the daughters (Video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Video 2.

claim: As the division completed, the daughter cells elongated on either side of the invading neighbor cell to occupy the full apical-basal axis in interphase.
source: Finally, as the division completed, the daughter cells elongated on either side of the invading neighbor cell to occupy the full apical-basal axis in interphase (Figure 1, Video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1 and Video 2.

claim: Notch1-expressing cells (which comprise all non-secretory cells including stem cells and absorptive cells) also interspersed during division.
source: Notch1-expressing cells (from Notch1CreERT2; R26RFP organoids), which comprise all non-secretory cells including stem cells and absorptive cells, also interspersed during division (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Dividing stem cells at the crypt base also separated, with secretory (Paneth) cells inserting between them.
source: Finally, dividing stem cells (labeled with Lgr5DTR-GFP) at the crypt base also separated, with secretory (Paneth) cells (labeled with Atoh1CreER; R26RFP) inserting between them (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, and Video 2.

claim: Altering cell fates by inhibiting Notch signaling to cause an expansion of secretory cells did not alter the frequency of interspersion.
source: Altering cell fates, for example by inhibiting Notch signaling to cause an expansion of secretory cells, did not alter the frequency of this process (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments manipulating Notch signaling, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Cells intersperse during a subset of divisions in all cell lineages of the crypt epithelium.
source: Thus, cells intersperse during a subset of divisions in all cell lineages of the crypt epithelium.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' imaging experiments across different cell lineages.

claim: A subset of progeny (18/40 progeny pairs) were interspersed with unlabeled cells or differently labeled cells in the intact intestine.
source: Consistent with our organoid imaging, we observed that a subset of progeny (18/40 progeny pairs, n = 3 mice) were interspersed with unlabeled cells or differently labeled cells in the intact intestine (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' in vivo experiments, with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: Progeny intersperse with neighboring cells in intestinal organoids and in the intestinal epithelium in vivo.
source: Thus, progeny intersperse with neighboring cells in intestinal organoids and in the intestinal epithelium in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' experiments in organoids and in vivo.

claim: The apical surface of the mitotic cell remained unperturbed: the apical footprint of the mitotic cell was similar to its interphase neighbors.
source: In contrast to the dramatic shape changes on the basal surface of dividing cells, the apical surface remained unperturbed: the apical footprint of the mitotic cell was similar to its interphase neighbors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), and a cytokinetic furrow was absent from the apical surface as in many metazoan epithelia (Fleming et al., 2007; Guillot and Lecuit, 2013; Herszterg et al., 2013; Founounou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C, and supported by citations to Fleming et al., 2007, Guillot and Lecuit, 2013, Herszterg et al., 2013, and Founounou et al., 2013.

claim: A cytokinetic furrow was absent from the apical surface as in many metazoan epithelia.
source: In contrast to the dramatic shape changes on the basal surface of dividing cells, the apical surface remained unperturbed: the apical footprint of the mitotic cell was similar to its interphase neighbors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), and a cytokinetic furrow was absent from the apical surface as in many metazoan epithelia (Fleming et al., 2007; Guillot and Lecuit, 2013; Herszterg et al., 2013; Founounou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C, and supported by citations to Fleming et al., 2007, Guillot and Lecuit, 2013, Herszterg et al., 2013, and Founounou et al., 2013.

claim: Previous studies showed that cell-cell junctions on the apical surface of the intestine persist throughout mitosis.
source: Previous studies showed that cell-cell junctions on the apical surface of the intestine persist throughout mitosis (Jinguji and Ishikawa, 1992) and staining with junctional markers indicated that the same is true for intestinal organoids (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jinguji and Ishikawa, 1992, and confirmed by the authors' experiments in organoids, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Staining with junctional markers indicated that cell-cell junctions persist throughout mitosis in intestinal organoids.
source: Previous studies showed that cell-cell junctions on the apical surface of the intestine persist throughout mitosis (Jinguji and Ishikawa, 1992) and staining with junctional markers indicated that the same is true for intestinal organoids (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cytokinesis occurred symmetrically in dissociated cells, in contrast to the polarized cytokinesis that occurs in the tissue.
source: In contrast to the polarized cytokinesis that occurs in the tissue, cytokinesis occurred symmetrically in dissociated cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—video 4), suggesting that tissue architecture plays a crucial role in this polarization.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments with dissociated cells, with reference to Figure 2B and Figure 2—video 4.

claim: Tissue architecture plays a crucial role in the polarization of cytokinesis.
source: In contrast to the polarized cytokinesis that occurs in the tissue, cytokinesis occurred symmetrically in dissociated cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—video 4), suggesting that tissue architecture plays a crucial role in this polarization.
evidence: This is inferred from the authors' experiments showing that cytokinesis is polarized in tissue but symmetric in dissociated cells.

claim: Mixing arises during cytokinesis as part of a suite of mitotic cell shape changes that are confined to the basolateral surface within the context of the tissue.
source: Together, these data indicate that mixing arises during cytokinesis as part of a suite of mitotic cell shape changes that are confined to the basolateral surface within the context of the tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' experiments.

claim: Apical displacement initiated concurrently with mitotic entry.
source: Apical displacement initiated concurrently with mitotic entry (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 3 and Figure 2—video 5), indicating that it was distinct from interkinetic nuclear migration, a process in which the nucleus is moved apically during interphase (interkinesis) (Sauer, 1936) by actin or microtubule-based forces (reviewed in [Norden, 2017]).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 3, and Figure 2—video 5.

claim: Apical displacement is distinct from interkinetic nuclear migration.
source: Apical displacement initiated concurrently with mitotic entry (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 3 and Figure 2—video 5), indicating that it was distinct from interkinetic nuclear migration, a process in which the nucleus is moved apically during interphase (interkinesis) (Sauer, 1936) by actin or microtubule-based forces (reviewed in [Norden, 2017]).
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of apical displacement (concurrent with mitotic entry) compared to interkinetic nuclear migration (during interphase), and supported by citations to Sauer, 1936 and Norden, 2017.

claim: Interkinetic nuclear migration is a process in which the nucleus is moved apically during interphase (interkinesis) by actin or microtubule-based forces.
source: Apical displacement initiated concurrently with mitotic entry (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 3 and Figure 2—video 5), indicating that it was distinct from interkinetic nuclear migration, a process in which the nucleus is moved apically during interphase (interkinesis) (Sauer, 1936) by actin or microtubule-based forces (reviewed in [Norden, 2017]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sauer, 1936 and Norden, 2017.

claim: Apical displacement occurred as cells adopted the rounded geometry classically associated with mitosis.
source: Apical displacement occurred as cells adopted the rounded geometry classically associated with mitosis (reviewed in [Théry and Bornens, 2008]) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 1, Figure 2—video 5, Figure 2—video 6); at metaphase and anaphase, only fine membranous processes tethered the cell to the basal surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F), consistent with previous observations (Carroll et al., 2017; Fleming et al., 2007; Jinguji and Ishikawa, 1992; Trier, 1963).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 1, Figure 2—video 5, and Figure 2—video 6, and supported by a citation to Théry and Bornens, 2008.

claim: At metaphase and anaphase, only fine membranous processes tethered the cell to the basal surface.
source: Apical displacement occurred as cells adopted the rounded geometry classically associated with mitosis (reviewed in [Théry and Bornens, 2008]) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 1, Figure 2—video 5, Figure 2—video 6); at metaphase and anaphase, only fine membranous processes tethered the cell to the basal surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F), consistent with previous observations (Carroll et al., 2017; Fleming et al., 2007; Jinguji and Ishikawa, 1992; Trier, 1963).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F, and supported by citations to Carroll et al., 2017, Fleming et al., 2007, Jinguji and Ishikawa, 1992, and Trier, 1963.

claim: Mitotic rounding contributes to late stages of interkinetic nuclear migration in some systems.
source: Mitotic rounding also contributes to late stages of interkinetic nuclear migration in some systems (Meyer et al., 2011; Spear and Erickson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Meyer et al., 2011 and Spear and Erickson, 2012.

claim: Treatment with the actin depolymerizing small molecule Latrunculin A disrupted rounding and apical displacement.
source: Treatment with the actin depolymerizing small molecule Latrunculin A disrupted rounding and apical displacement (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—video 7); in contrast, cells treated with the microtubule depolymerizing drug nocodazole rounded onto the apical surface similarly to control cells (Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—video 8, Figure 2—video 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' pharmacological experiments, with reference to Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—video 7.

claim: Cells treated with the microtubule depolymerizing drug nocodazole rounded onto the apical surface similarly to control cells.
source: Treatment with the actin depolymerizing small molecule Latrunculin A disrupted rounding and apical displacement (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—video 7); in contrast, cells treated with the microtubule depolymerizing drug nocodazole rounded onto the apical surface similarly to control cells (Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—video 8, Figure 2—video 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' pharmacological experiments, with reference to Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—video 8, and Figure 2—video 9.

claim: As Latrunculin-treated cells entered anaphase, the chromosome masses were positioned orthogonally to the plane of the epithelium, in contrast to the planar divisions observed in control cells.
source: As Latrunculin-treated cells entered anaphase, the chromosome masses were positioned orthogonally to the plane of the epithelium, in contrast to the planar divisions observed in control cells (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, Figure 2—videos 7, 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' pharmacological experiments, with reference to Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, and Figure 2—videos 7, 9.

claim: Cell rounding is crucial for the normal planar orientation of the spindle in the intestine.
source: This suggests that cell rounding is crucial for the normal planar orientation of the spindle in the intestine, as in some Drosophila epithelia (Chanet et al., 2017; Nakajima et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the authors' experiments showing that disrupting cell rounding leads to non-planar spindle orientation, and supported by citations to Chanet et al., 2017 and Nakajima et al., 2013.

claim: Actin-based cell rounding displaces mitotic cells apically and is required for planar spindle orientation.
source: Collectively, our data suggest that actin-based cell rounding displaces mitotic cells apically and is required for planar spindle orientation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' pharmacological experiments.

claim: The basal edge of nascent daughters extended a protrusive front that resembled the leading edge of migrating cells.
source: After division, we observed that the basal edge of nascent daughters extended a protrusive front that resembled the leading edge of migrating cells (Figure 2G; Figure 2—video 10).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 2G and Figure 2—video 10.

claim: Mitotic exit and reversal of CDK phosphorylation are sufficient for basal reinsertion, even in the absence of chromosome segregation.
source: Cells arrested in mitosis did not reinsert unless mitotic exit was induced by inhibition of the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC; Mps1 inhibitor AZ3146) or cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK; RO-3306) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, Figure 2—video 11). Thus, mitotic exit and reversal of CDK phosphorylation are sufficient for basal reinsertion, even in the absence of chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' pharmacological experiments, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1H and Figure 2—video 11.

claim: When the actin cytoskeleton was disrupted and mitotic exit was induced, the nucleus reformed its interphase morphology on the apical surface and the cell boundary did not protrude toward the basal surface.
source: When we disrupted the actin cytoskeleton and induced mitotic exit, the nucleus reformed its interphase morphology on the apical surface and the cell boundary did not protrude toward the basal surface (Figure 2H,I, Figure 2—video 12).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' pharmacological experiments, with reference to Figure 2H,I and Figure 2—video 12.

claim: Depolymerizing microtubules with nocodazole and inducing mitotic exit did not interfere with the ability of nuclei or the cell boundary to reach the basal surface.
source: In contrast, depolymerizing microtubules with nocodazole and inducing mitotic exit did not interfere with the ability of nuclei or the cell boundary to reach the basal surface (Figure 2H,I, Figure 2—video 13).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' pharmacological experiments, with reference to Figure 2H,I and Figure 2—video 13.

claim: Nuclei reinserted normally following inhibition of cytokinesis using the Polo-like kinase one inhibitor, BI2536.
source: Although actin also plays a critical role in cytokinesis, nuclei reinserted normally following inhibition of cytokinesis using the Polo-like kinase one inhibitor, BI2536 (Lénárt et al., 2007; Steegmaier et al., 2007) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), indicating that cytokinesis is dispensable for basal movement.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' pharmacological experiments, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1J, and supported by citations to Lénárt et al., 2007 and Steegmaier et al., 2007.

claim: Cytokinesis is dispensable for basal movement.
source: Although actin also plays a critical role in cytokinesis, nuclei reinserted normally following inhibition of cytokinesis using the Polo-like kinase one inhibitor, BI2536 (Lénárt et al., 2007; Steegmaier et al., 2007) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), indicating that cytokinesis is dispensable for basal movement.
evidence: This is inferred from the authors' experiments showing that nuclei reinsert normally when cytokinesis is inhibited.

claim: Actin-driven cell elongation after mitotic exit re-establishes the interphase architecture of daughter cells.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that actin-driven cell elongation after mitotic exit re-establishes the interphase architecture of daughter cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' pharmacological experiments.

claim: Fetal spheroids did not exhibit apical-basal mitotic movements and the daughters did not intersperse with other cells during division (50/50 divisions).
source: Fetal spheroids did not exhibit apical-basal mitotic movements and the daughters did not intersperse with other cells during division (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—video 1, Figure 3—video 2) (50/50 divisions).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' imaging experiments in fetal spheroids, with reference to Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—video 1, and Figure 3—video 2.

claim: Adult spheroids cultured in exogenous Wnt failed to exhibit apical-basal mitotic movements and the daughters did not intermix with other cells (50/50 divisions).
source: These adult spheroids also failed to exhibit apical-basal mitotic movements and the daughters did not intermix with other cells (50/50 divisions) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' imaging experiments in adult spheroids, with reference to Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Adult spheroids cultured in high Wnt conditions contained patches of cellular progeny, in contrast to the interspersed pattern of cell lineages observed in normal adult organoids.
source: Consistent with the lack of interspersion, these spheroids contained patches of cellular progeny (Figure 3C), in contrast to the interspersed pattern of cell lineages observed in normal adult organoids (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments, with reference to Figure 3C and Figure 1A.

claim: A subset of organoids cultured in high Wnt conditions retained their budded morphology and elongated apical-basal cell shape; these organoids continued to exhibit apical displacement and the interspersed pattern of cell lineages.
source: As an internal control, a subset of organoids cultured in high Wnt conditions retained their budded morphology and elongated apical-basal cell shape; these organoids continued to exhibit apical displacement and the interspersed pattern of cell lineages (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments, with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The effect of cell shape on interspersion is separable from hyperactive Wnt signaling.
source: This experiment, as well as our observations of adjacent progeny in the fetal spheroids, which exhibit very low expression of the Wnt reporter gene Axin2 (Mustata et al., 2013), indicate that the effect of cell shape on interspersion is separable from hyperactive Wnt signaling, in contrast with previous work (Carroll et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' experiments in spheroids with different Wnt signaling levels, and supported by a citation to Mustata et al., 2013.

claim: An elongated apical-basal axis is critical for apical mitosis and cell interspersion during division.
source: Together, these data indicate that an elongated apical-basal axis is critical for apical mitosis and cell interspersion during division.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' experiments manipulating cellular aspect ratio.

claim: Pioneering work by Gardner and Cockroft (1998) revealed that cells injected into mouse blastocysts to generate chimeras become dispersed throughout the epiblast and primitive ectoderm of the post-implantation embryo.
source: Pioneering work by Gardner and Cockroft (1998) revealed that cells injected into mouse blastocysts to generate chimeras become dispersed throughout the epiblast and primitive ectoderm of the post-implantation embryo.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gardner and Cockroft, 1998.

claim: Gardner and Cockroft (1998) proposed that the dispersed pattern of cells in the epiblast and primitive ectoderm might arise as a consequence of cell division, which they and others have observed occurs on the apical surface of the tissue.
source: The authors proposed that this pattern might arise as a consequence of cell division, which they and others have observed occurs on the apical surface of the tissue (Gardner and Cockroft, 1998; Ichikawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gardner and Cockroft, 1998 and Ichikawa et al., 2013.

claim: Divisions in the epiblast/primitive ectoderm of E7.5 mouse embryos proceeded in a similar manner to the intestinal epithelium, with mitotic cells displacing to the apical surface as they rounded.
source: We imaged cell divisions in these embryos for at least 3 hr and observed that divisions proceeded in a similar manner to the intestinal epithelium, with mitotic cells displacing to the apical surface as they rounded (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments in early mouse embryos, with reference to Figure 3F–G.

claim: Daughter cells in the epiblast/primitive ectoderm separated from one another and interspersed with unlabeled cells during cytokinesis (8/10 divisions, n = 3 embryos from three pregnancies).
source: Daughter cells then separated from one another and interspersed with unlabeled cells during cytokinesis (Figure 3H, Video 4) (8/10 divisions, n = 3 embryos from three pregnancies).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' imaging experiments in early mouse embryos, with reference to Figure 3H and Video 4.

claim: Daughter cells positioned on the apical surface intersperse with other cells during cytokinesis in the elongated epiblast/primitive ectoderm of the embryo, as in the adult small intestine.
source: Thus, daughter cells positioned on the apical surface intersperse with other cells during cytokinesis in the elongated epiblast/primitive ectoderm of the embryo, as in the adult small intestine.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' imaging experiments in early mouse embryos.

claim: The cells of the visceral endoderm (the low aspect ratio cells that surround the epiblast) did not exhibit apical displacement and daughters remain adjacent (12/12 divisions, n = 3 embryos from three pregnancies).
source: In contrast, the cells of the visceral endoderm (the low aspect ratio cells that surround the epiblast) did not exhibit apical displacement and daughters remain adjacent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—video 3, 12/12 divisions, n = 3 embryos from three pregnancies), consistent with classical experiments reporting outgrowth of contiguous clones in this tissue (Gardner, 1984; 1985; Lawson et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' imaging experiments in early mouse embryos, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Figure 3—video 3, and supported by citations to Gardner, 1984, 1985, and Lawson et al., 1991.

claim: Classical experiments reported outgrowth of contiguous clones in the visceral endoderm.
source: In contrast, the cells of the visceral endoderm (the low aspect ratio cells that surround the epiblast) did not exhibit apical displacement and daughters remain adjacent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—video 3, 12/12 divisions, n = 3 embryos from three pregnancies), consistent with classical experiments reporting outgrowth of contiguous clones in this tissue (Gardner, 1984; 1985; Lawson et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gardner, 1984, 1985, and Lawson et al., 1991.

claim: Cell division generates distinct progeny patterns in the two layers of the early post-implantation mouse embryo, consistent with a central role for cellular aspect ratio in determining the spatial patterning of cell progeny.
source: Thus, cell division generates distinct progeny patterns in the two layers of the early post-implantation mouse embryo, consistent with a central role for cellular aspect ratio in determining the spatial patterning of cell progeny.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' imaging experiments in early mouse embryos.

claim: Intermixing arises when a neighboring cell inserts between apically displaced daughter cells during cytokinesis.
source: Here, we show that intermixing arises when a neighboring cell inserts between apically displaced daughter cells during cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the authors' experiments.

claim: The process of intermixing requires that the neighboring cell and dividing cell are positioned in such a way that the neighbor can occupy the wedge between the daughters generated by the ingressing furrow.
source: The process of intermixing requires that the neighboring cell and dividing cell are positioned in such a way that the neighbor can occupy the wedge between the daughters generated by the ingressing furrow.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' experiments.

claim: The neighboring cell can become opportunely positioned for invasion into the cytokinetic furrow as a consequence of the cell shape changes associated with vertebrate mitosis in tissues comprised of cells with a high aspect ratio.
source: Our data support a model in which the neighboring cell can become opportunely positioned for invasion into the cytokinetic furrow as a consequence of the cell shape changes associated with vertebrate mitosis in tissues comprised of cells with a high aspect ratio (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their data, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: In cells with a high aspect ratio, the actin-driven cell shape changes required for mitosis (rounding and subsequent elongation) displace the dividing cell along the apical-basal axis.
source: In cells with a high aspect ratio, the actin-driven cell shape changes required for mitosis (rounding and subsequent elongation) displace the dividing cell along the apical-basal axis (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their data, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: As a result of apical displacement, an elongated interphase neighboring cell can surround the dividing cell both basally and laterally, allowing it to follow the path of the ingressing furrow between the daughters.
source: As a result, an elongated interphase neighboring cell can surround the dividing cell both basally and laterally, allowing it to follow the path of the ingressing furrow between the daughters.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their data.

claim: Live imaging of cell division in the two epithelial layers of the peri-gastrulation mouse embryo supports a model in which cell aspect ratio is a critical parameter for determining whether cellular progeny intersperse.
source: Consistent with a key role for cell aspect ratio in interspersion behavior, reducing the aspect ratio in organoids generates patches. Live imaging of cell division in the two epithelial layers of the peri-gastrulation mouse embryo further supports a model in which cell aspect ratio is a critical parameter for determining whether cellular progeny intersperse, raising the intriguing possibility that the patterning principles that we define in the intestine may be a common feature of many mammalian epithelia.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' experiments in early mouse embryos.

claim: The patterning principles defined in the intestine may be a common feature of many mammalian epithelia.
source: Consistent with a key role for cell aspect ratio in interspersion behavior, reducing the aspect ratio in organoids generates patches. Live imaging of cell division in the two epithelial layers of the peri-gastrulation mouse embryo further supports a model in which cell aspect ratio is a critical parameter for determining whether cellular progeny intersperse, raising the intriguing possibility that the patterning principles that we define in the intestine may be a common feature of many mammalian epithelia.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the authors' findings in intestinal organoids and early mouse embryos.

claim: Interspersion arises as a mechanical consequence of executing planar cell division in elongated cells, rather than being determined by developmental signaling or differential adhesion between cells.
source: Several lines of evidence support a model in which interspersion arises as a mechanical consequence of executing planar cell division in elongated cells, rather than being determined by developmental signaling or differential adhesion between cells.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their data.

claim: Daughter separation is observed throughout the intestinal crypt for all progenitor cell identities: stem cells, Notch-expressing absorptive progenitors and Atoh1-expressing secretory progenitors.
source: First, daughter separation is observed throughout the intestinal crypt for all progenitor cell identities: stem cells, Notch-expressing absorptive progenitors and Atoh1-expressing secretory progenitors (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Daughter separation is a frequent but not universal event, occurring in approximately half of the divisions observed.
source: However, importantly, daughter separation is a frequent but not universal event, occurring in approximately half of the divisions observed, including when observing cells of a specific lineage (Figure 1, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' imaging experiments, with reference to Figure 1 and Figure 3D.

claim: Altering epithelial geometry in culture disrupts interspersion.
source: In contrast, altering epithelial geometry in culture disrupts interspersion (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments manipulating epithelial geometry, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The mechanisms of interspersion defined for the intestinal epithelium may be generalizable to other vertebrate tissues with similar physical parameters.
source: Since our data indicate that interspersion can arise from the execution of planar cell division coupled with the physical parameters of the tissue, it raises the possibility that the mechanisms of interspersion that we define for the intestinal epithelium may be generalizable to other vertebrate tissues with similar physical parameters.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the authors' findings.

claim: Several tissues across vertebrates with a high aspect ratio have been reported to exhibit division-coupled interspersion.
source: Consistent with this notion, we observed similar interspersion in the high aspect ratio epithelium of the early mouse embryo, while the surrounding low aspect ratio epithelium did not exhibit division-coupled interspersion (Figure 3). Several tissues across vertebrates with a high aspect ratio have also been reported to exhibit division-coupled interspersion (Carroll et al., 2017; Firmino et al., 2016; Gardner and Cockroft, 1998; Higashi et al., 2016; Packard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carroll et al., 2017, Firmino et al., 2016, Gardner and Cockroft, 1998, Higashi et al., 2016, and Packard et al., 2013.

claim: In numerous tissues in which cells have a low aspect ratio, progeny remain adjacent and form contiguous patches, including the interfollicular epidermis, MDCK cells, and alveolar epithelial cells.
source: In contrast, in numerous tissues in which cells have a low aspect ratio, progeny remain adjacent and form contiguous patches, including the interfollicular epidermis (Ouspenskaia et al., 2016; Rompolas et al., 2016), MDCK cells (Reinsch and Karsenti, 1994), and alveolar epithelial cells (Desai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ouspenskaia et al., 2016, Rompolas et al., 2016, Reinsch and Karsenti, 1994, and Desai et al., 2014.

claim: Isolated reports of division-coupled interspersion in diverse vertebrates including frog, chick and mouse may be unified by a common physical mechanism arising from the aspect ratio of the tissue and the mechanics of cell division.
source: Our model raises the possibility that isolated reports of division-coupled interspersion in diverse vertebrates including frog, chick and mouse may be unified by a common physical mechanism arising from the aspect ratio of the tissue and the mechanics of cell division.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the authors' model.

claim: In vertebrates, the mechanism of furrow ingression minimizes the contact between the daughters and progresses until a single apex physically connects the two cells.
source: In vertebrates, the mechanism of furrow ingression minimizes the contact between the daughters and progresses until a single apex physically connects the two cells (Higashi et al., 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Higashi et al., 2016, and by the authors' data, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The development of the furrow creates a position, both basally and laterally, for neighboring cells to invade and occupy.
source: An important component of our model is that the development of the furrow creates a position, both basally and laterally, for neighboring cells to invade and occupy.
evidence: This is a component of the authors' model.

claim: During cytokinesis in Drosophila, the two daughters form a long adhesive contact between them.
source: However, in contrast, during cytokinesis in Drosophila, the two daughters form a long adhesive contact between them (Gibson et al., 2006) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), dependent on myosin II accumulation in the neighboring cells (Herszterg et al., 2013; Pinheiro et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gibson et al., 2006, Herszterg et al., 2013, and Pinheiro et al., 2017, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The long adhesive contact between daughters in Drosophila is dependent on myosin II accumulation in the neighboring cells.
source: However, in contrast, during cytokinesis in Drosophila, the two daughters form a long adhesive contact between them (Gibson et al., 2006) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), dependent on myosin II accumulation in the neighboring cells (Herszterg et al., 2013; Pinheiro et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herszterg et al., 2013 and Pinheiro et al., 2017.

claim: Drosophila epithelia exhibit a high aspect ratio, apical mitosis and non-concentric cytokinesis, yet do not exhibit cell interspersion and form contiguous patches of progeny.
source: In this regard, it is interesting to note that Drosophila epithelia exhibit a high aspect ratio, apical mitosis and non-concentric cytokinesis, yet do not exhibit cell interspersion and form contiguous patches of progeny (Bryant, 1970; Bryant and Schneiderman, 1969; Founounou et al., 2013; Gibson et al., 2006; Guillot and Lecuit, 2013; Herszterg et al., 2013; Meyer et al., 2011; Morais-de-Sá and Sunkel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bryant, 1970, Bryant and Schneiderman, 1969, Founounou et al., 2013, Gibson et al., 2006, Guillot and Lecuit, 2013, Herszterg et al., 2013, Meyer et al., 2011, and Morais-de-Sá and Sunkel, 2013.

claim: The extended cell-cell contact formed between daughter cells in Drosophila would oppose the invasion of a neighboring cell.
source: We speculate that the extended cell-cell contact formed between daughter cells in Drosophila would oppose the invasion of a neighboring cell.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the authors' model.

claim: Cell interspersion is unlikely to be unique to those tissues in which it has been reported, since it requires a set of criteria that are satisfied by many vertebrate epithelia.
source: Broadly, since our data suggest that cell interspersion requires a set of criteria that are satisfied by many vertebrate epithelia, it is unlikely to be unique to those tissues in which it has been reported.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the authors' findings.

claim: The numerous elongated pseudostratified epithelia that undergo apical mitosis due to interkinetic nuclear migration are particularly attractive candidates for division-coupled interspersion.
source: Although our work has focused on the columnar epithelium of the small intestine, in which mitotic cell shape changes are sufficient to displace dividing cells relative to their neighbors, the numerous elongated pseudostratified epithelia that undergo apical mitosis due to interkinetic nuclear migration (reviewed in [Norden, 2017]) are particularly attractive candidates for division-coupled interspersion.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the authors' findings, and supported by a citation to Norden, 2017.

claim: Interspersion during cell division may be widespread across elongated vertebrate epithelia.
source: Together, our model suggests that interspersion during cell division may be widespread across elongated vertebrate epithelia.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the authors' model.
